title: 1.3.19 Document a Messy Program
description: Twelve lines with no comments, no spacing and terrible names. Fix it to the class style guide and write the README. Auto-graded.

steps.title: Rename everything
steps.instructions: Replace the single-letter names with descriptive camelCase names. The program calculates a book order: use bookTitle, unitPrice, quantity, subtotal and orderTotal, and make the tax rate a constant named taxRate.

steps.title: Fix the formatting
steps.instructions: Style guide: one space around every operator, a semicolon on every statement, and a blank line between logical sections.

steps.title: Comment every non-obvious line
steps.instructions: Add inline // comments explaining what each calculation is for. Explain why, not just what the symbols do.

steps.title: Write the README
steps.instructions: Open README.md and answer the three headings that are already there -- one sentence or one bullet each is enough, as long as it actually says something. Under the last one, mention the tax rate: it is the number most likely to need changing later.

requirements.title: taxRate is declared with const
requirements.description: The rate that never changes is declared with const, not let. Help: 1.3.2 (camelCase and const)

requirements.title: bookTitle holds the title
requirements.description: Declares bookTitle with quoted text. Help: 1.3.6 (Human-Readable Names)

requirements.title: unitPrice and quantity are named
requirements.description: Declares both unitPrice and quantity. Help: 1.3.6 (Human-Readable Names)

requirements.title: subtotal is computed from them
requirements.description: subtotal is unitPrice times quantity. Help: 1.3.6 (Human-Readable Names)

requirements.title: orderTotal uses the tax rate
requirements.description: orderTotal is computed from subtotal and taxRate. Help: 1.3.6 (Human-Readable Names)

requirements.title: No single-letter variables remain
requirements.description: No declaration of a one-letter variable is left in the file. Help: 1.3.6 (Human-Readable Names)

requirements.title: Operators are spaced
requirements.description: No cramped arithmetic like a*b remains: every operator has a space on each side. Help: 1.3.3 (Code Layout)

requirements.title: At least four explanatory comments
requirements.description: Four or more comments explaining the code, written as // or /* */. Help: 1.3.4 (Comments: // and /* */)

requirements.title: README answers all three prompts
requirements.description: Each of the three headings has a real answer under it -- a sentence or a bullet, not an empty heading. Help: 1.3.18 (What a README Is For)

requirements.title: README mentions the tax rate
requirements.description: README tells the reader about the tax rate they may need to change. Help: 1.3.6 (Human-Readable Names)

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code and README
aiCheck.prompt: The student worked on the lab "1.3.19 Document a Messy Program". The task they were given: a twelve-line program with no comments, no spacing and terrible names. Fix it to the class style guide (descriptive camelCase names, const for a value that never changes, spaces around operators, at least four explanatory comments) and write a short README.md that answers three prompts. You are given TWO files in one message: script.js first, then a line reading ----- README.md ----- followed by the README. Criteria about names, operators and comments are about script.js; the README criteria are about the README. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable and function names, template strings, arrow functions, semicolons, spacing, quotes and order are all fine. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment never runs. Write each note for THIS student's own code: in a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.
